question: What did you like most about this prompt?
answer: It is concrete and checkable. The This computer section told me exactly which browsers, tools and limits I had, so I could test the engine and hub for real instead of guessing, and the hub harness gives a plain pass or fail. It also left the creative calls (genre, perspective, how much to research) to me while being strict about what done means: a dev mode with sliders, attract mode at 10 seconds, the 10-foot UI, music at 10%, and an exit interview with a fixed shape. That made the plan easy to make complete, because I could check it line by line against the brief.

question: What was confusing?
answer: Three things. First, the Multiplayer line, 'for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own': it can mean the game must simply still run outside a session, or that it needs multiplayer without the hub. I couldn't settle it, so the plan does both, with a split-screen mode. Second, TASK.md is written to the builder while I was the planner: the title process, the file names, the exit interview and the chat reply are all addressed to someone else, and the goal says PLAN.md must cover everything TASK.md asks. I had to decide what 'cover' means for things only a builder can do, and I settled on telling the builder where each one goes. Third, some instructions pull against the materials: the brief prefers file:// while the engine guide says ES modules don't load from file://, and 'keep the engine as it ships' sits next to a single-HTML deliverable. Both only resolved once I tried bundling. The title as a riff on the source's name, in a game that must not be a recreation, also leaves open how close a riff may get.

question: What was the hardest thing to do?
answer: Choosing how much to decide for the builders without knowing who they are or what budget they have. The plan had to work for builders I can't talk to, so anything risky needed to be settled rather than described. The hardest single part was the driving model: the engine's Vehicle is arcade-level, so I had to design a car model that makes tuning felt and keep it stable. Getting there meant finding and fixing a weave, then spins under braking, then sliding wide, before all 14 cars lapped all six tracks in a scripted test. Even so, no human has driven it, and I could not judge how it feels on a real pad, so the plan says so. The other hard part was length: every section I added made the plan safer to build from and longer to read, and it ended up large, at about 120 KB including code.

question: What would you change in this prompt?
answer: Say who the builders are and roughly what budget they have, so a plan can be pitched at the right depth and scope. Say whether a plan may include working code and data, and give a size limit if there is one. Spell out the on-its-own multiplayer requirement in one sentence. Mark which parts of TASK.md are for the builder only, or give the planner a version with those removed, and say how 'covers everything' applies to them. Add a line to the brief or the kit saying that a bundled, inlined build is the expected way to reach a single HTML on file://, since that one question decides the whole build pipeline. Also say whether planners may leave their experiments behind for builders: I deleted mine and moved what mattered into the plan, but sharing a tested starter project would save everyone work.
